subtopic_detail: Persistent head lice after repeated insecticide use and the significance of live versus hatched eggs
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A mother brings her 6 year old daughter in frustrated because the school has sent her home twice. She has used a pyrethrin containing lotion three times over five weeks, each time as a single application, and says she still finds moving insects in the hair two days after each treatment.

The mother has not treated anyone else in the house. On wet combing you recover four live lice and numerous eggs, of which the ones close to the scalp are brown and full and those more than two centimetres out along the shaft are pale and empty. The scalp skin is intact with no pustules, crusting or tender nodes.

data_table.Examination: Four live adult lice recovered on wet combing, viable eggs within 1 cm of the scalp, empty egg cases distally, no excoriation or secondary infection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe oral ivermectin for the child and treat the household contacts at the same time
options.rationale: Oral ivermectin is held in reserve for infestation that has failed correctly applied topical treatment, and treatment here has never included the repeat application (Source: RCH CPG: Head Lice; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Advise hot washing of all bedding and clothing and repeat the same lotion in seven days
options.rationale: Environmental decontamination adds nothing because lice die within a day off the scalp, and repeating an agent that has already failed three times ignores the likely resistance (Source: RCH CPG: Head Lice).

options.text: Reassure that the remaining eggs are not viable and that no further treatment is needed
options.rationale: Empty cases along the shaft are indeed the residue of past infestation, but full brown eggs within a centimetre of the scalp plus live adults confirm ongoing active infestation (Source: RCH CPG: Head Lice).

options.text: Prescribe oral trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole for ten days and recheck the scalp afterwards
options.rationale: Systemic antibacterial therapy treats secondary bacterial infection of an excoriated scalp, and the skin here is intact with no pustules or lymphadenopathy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Switch to a dimeticone preparation applied twice seven days apart with weekly wet combing
options.rationale: Repeated failure of a neurotoxic insecticide points to resistance, and a physically acting dimeticone applied twice a week apart covers the eggs that hatch after the first application (Source: RCH CPG: Head Lice; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Head lice treatment fails far more often from technique than from true resistance, and the commonest error is a single application, because no topical product reliably kills eggs and the survivors hatch six to seven days later. Australian guidance is therefore for two applications seven days apart with whichever agent is used, combined with regular wet conditioner combing to confirm cure. Physically acting agents such as dimeticone smother the louse rather than poisoning it, so resistance to pyrethrins and other neurotoxic insecticides does not apply. Distinguishing live eggs near the scalp from empty cases further out prevents the common trap of retreating a child who has already been cured.
key_points: Any topical agent needs two applications seven days apart to catch newly hatched lice
Empty egg cases more than 1 cm from the scalp are old and do not indicate active infestation
Dimeticone acts physically so insecticide resistance does not apply to it
Treat other household members only if live lice are found on them
Australian school policy does not exclude children with head lice once treatment has begun
explanation.pearls: Hair grows about 1 cm a month, so an egg found more than 1 cm from the scalp was laid over a month ago and is almost always an empty case rather than evidence of treatment failure.

subtopic_detail: Referral urgency for a newly constant convergent squint in a preschool child
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 3 year old girl whose grandmother says her left eye has started turning in towards her nose. It was only occasional when she was tired six months ago but is now there all the time, and she has begun tilting her head and closing that eye in bright light.

On cover testing the left eye moves outwards to take up fixation when the right is covered. The corneal light reflex sits lateral to the centre of the left pupil. Red reflexes are present, equal and normal in both eyes, and eye movements are full in all directions with no proptosis. Her parents have been told by a friend that squints get better on their own by school age.

data_table.Examination: Constant left convergent deviation, cover test shows outward refixation movement of the left eye, symmetrical normal red reflexes, full extraocular movements
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed in the practice

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits before any referral
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is driven by a restricted eye movement, papilloedema, an abnormal red reflex or other neurological signs, none of which is present here (Source: RCH CPG: Squint).

options.text: Refer to a paediatric ophthalmologist now for refraction and amblyopia assessment
options.rationale: A constant squint at any age needs assessment because the deviating eye is being suppressed, and treatment of the resulting amblyopia works far better before visual maturity is complete (Source: RCH CPG: Squint).

options.text: Reassure the family that most squints of this type resolve and review her before school
options.rationale: Intermittent deviation in the first few months of life may resolve, but a constant squint that has progressed over six months in a 3 year old will not and waiting costs treatable vision (Source: RCH CPG: Squint).

options.text: Start patching of the right eye for two hours daily and reassess in three months
options.rationale: Occlusion therapy is part of amblyopia treatment but it follows cycloplegic refraction, since correcting a hypermetropic error alone resolves a proportion of these squints (Source: RCH CPG: Squint).

options.text: Refer to an optometrist for glasses and review the alignment again in six months
options.rationale: Refraction is essential but a child with a constant squint needs the orthoptic and ophthalmological assessment that also grades and treats amblyopia (Source: RCH CPG: Squint).

explanation.summary: A squint matters because the developing brain suppresses the image from the deviating eye, and that suppression becomes irreversible as the visual cortex matures through early childhood. Intermittent deviation in the first three to four months of life is common and often resolves, but any squint that is constant, that appears after six months of age, or that is progressing needs specialist assessment rather than observation. The two findings that turn a routine referral into an urgent one are an abnormal or absent red reflex, which raises retinoblastoma or cataract, and a restricted eye movement with other neurological signs. Much paediatric convergent squint is driven by uncorrected long sightedness, so cycloplegic refraction comes before any decision about patching or surgery.
key_points: Any constant squint, or any squint after six months of age, warrants specialist referral
The cover test demonstrates the deviation by showing refixation of the uncovered eye
An abnormal red reflex makes the referral immediate rather than routine
Cycloplegic refraction precedes patching because glasses alone correct some deviations
Amblyopia treatment is far more effective the earlier in childhood it starts
explanation.pearls: The corneal light reflex sits lateral to the pupil centre in a convergent squint and medial to it in a divergent one, which lets you identify the direction of deviation in a child too young to cooperate with cover testing.

subtopic_detail: Infant with fixed head turning preference and the associated screening obligation
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a community clinic. A 10 week old boy is brought in because he always looks to the right and his mother cannot get him to feed comfortably on one side. She noticed a firm lump in the side of his neck at about four weeks that has not changed since.

He was born at term by breech extraction at caesarean section and was the first baby. There is a firm non tender 2 cm swelling within the left sternocleidomastoid. His head rests tilted towards the left shoulder with the chin turned to the right, and passive rotation of the chin to the left stops at 45 degrees. The lump does not transilluminate, the overlying skin is normal and he is thriving on the 75th centile.

data_table.Examination: Firm 2 cm intramuscular swelling in the left sternocleidomastoid, left head tilt with right chin rotation, passive left rotation limited to 45 degrees, symmetrical Moro and normal tone in all four limbs

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange fine needle aspiration of the neck swelling and refer to paediatric surgery
options.rationale: Aspiration is for a mass that is growing, cystic, inflamed or associated with systemic features, whereas a static firm swelling within the muscle belly with a matching postural deformity does not need sampling (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis).

options.text: Refer for physiotherapy and reassess the range of neck rotation again in three months
options.rationale: Physiotherapy is the correct treatment but a three month interval is too long at this age, and referring without the hip assessment leaves the associated condition unlooked for (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis).

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine to exclude a bony anomaly
options.rationale: Spinal imaging is indicated when the tilt is painful, of later onset, associated with neurological signs, or has no palpable muscle abnormality (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis).

options.text: Refer for physiotherapy and arrange a hip ultrasound to screen for dysplasia
options.rationale: The muscle swelling with restricted contralateral rotation is congenital muscular torticollis, and the same intrauterine crowding raises hip dysplasia risk enough that ultrasound screening is indicated alongside stretching (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis; RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Reassure the mother that the head position will correct itself once he starts to sit
options.rationale: Untreated restriction produces facial asymmetry and persistent head tilt, and outcomes from stretching are best when it begins in the first three months (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis).

explanation.summary: Congenital muscular torticollis presents in the first weeks as a fixed preference to look one way, with the head tilted towards the affected muscle and the chin rotated away from it, and often with a firm fibrous swelling within the sternocleidomastoid belly. The reason it cannot simply be referred to physiotherapy in isolation is that it shares its risk factors with developmental dysplasia of the hip, namely breech position, first pregnancy and intrauterine crowding, and hip dysplasia is present in a clinically important minority of these infants. Australian practice is therefore to arrange a hip ultrasound at the same time as the physiotherapy referral, using ultrasound rather than radiography because the femoral head is still cartilaginous before about four to six months. Stretching started in the first months resolves the great majority, while delay leads to fixed contracture, facial asymmetry and occasionally surgical release.
key_points: The head tilts towards the tight muscle and the chin rotates away from it
Breech presentation and first pregnancy are shared risk factors with hip dysplasia
Arrange hip ultrasound rather than radiography before about four to six months of age
Early stretching resolves most cases and avoids later facial asymmetry
Painful, late onset or neurologically abnormal torticollis needs imaging instead
explanation.pearls: Any infant diagnosed with congenital muscular torticollis should have a hip ultrasound, because dysplasia is found in roughly one in five and the hip examination alone misses a dysplastic but reduced hip.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

subtopic_detail: Chronic wet cough in a preschool child unresponsive to escalating asthma preventer therapy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the respiratory clinic. A 3 year old girl has coughed every day for nine weeks. Her mother says it is a rattly cough that sounds like it is bringing something up, that it is worse first thing in the morning, and that it does not wake her at night.

She was started on an inhaled corticosteroid six weeks ago and the dose has since been doubled with no change. She has never wheezed, has never needed a reliever for breathlessness, and has never choked on food or a toy. She was born at term, is fully immunised, is growing along the 50th centile and has normal stools. Her chest is clear today with no wheeze, crackles or clubbing, and a chest radiograph taken last week was reported as normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104, blood pressure 92/56, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Wet sounding cough on request, chest clear with no wheeze or crackles, no digital clubbing, normal growth centiles
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph reported as normal; sweat test not performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe amoxicillin clavulanate for two weeks and review the cough at the end of it
options.rationale: A daily wet cough for more than four weeks with no pointers to another diagnosis is treated as protracted bacterial bronchitis, and a two week course of a beta lactam with beta lactamase cover resolves the majority (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children

options.text: Double the inhaled corticosteroid again and add a leukotriene receptor antagonist
options.rationale: Further preventer escalation in a child who has never wheezed and has not responded to two dose steps repeats a failed trial and exposes her to growth and behavioural effects (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children).
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children

options.text: Arrange flexible bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage before any further treatment
options.rationale: Bronchoscopy is reserved for cough that fails two antibiotic courses or that suggests an inhaled foreign body or airway malacia, and no antibiotic trial has yet been given (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children).
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children

options.text: Start a proton pump inhibitor for eight weeks and review the response to treatment
options.rationale: Acid suppression for cough without other reflux features does not outperform placebo in children and delays a treatment that would work (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children).
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children

options.text: Request a sweat chloride test and a high resolution chest tomography scan this week
options.rationale: Suppurative lung disease is pursued when there is faltering growth, clubbing, abnormal stools or a persistent radiographic abnormality, none of which is present in this well grown child (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children).
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children

explanation.summary: Chronic cough in children is defined as a daily cough lasting more than four weeks, and the first branch point is whether it is wet or dry, because that single feature reorganises the differential. A wet cough in a child who is otherwise well and growing normally is most often protracted bacterial bronchitis, caused by a biofilm of Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae or Moraxella catarrhalis in the large airways. It is treated with two weeks of amoxicillin clavulanate, extended to four weeks if the response is partial, and it is important to recognise because untreated recurrent episodes progress to bronchiectasis. Persistent failure after two courses, or the presence of clubbing, faltering growth or radiographic change, moves the child towards bronchoscopy and investigation for cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia or immunodeficiency.
key_points: Chronic cough in children means daily cough for more than four weeks
A wet cough without wheeze is not asthma and does not respond to preventer escalation
Protracted bacterial bronchitis is treated with two weeks of amoxicillin clavulanate
Failure of two antibiotic courses is the trigger for bronchoscopy and further workup
Untreated recurrent protracted bacterial bronchitis can progress to bronchiectasis
explanation.pearls: Ask the parent whether the cough sounds wet or dry rather than whether the child brings up sputum, since preschool children swallow secretions and the parental description of a rattly cough is the practical substitute for observed sputum.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic Cough in Children

subtopic_detail: Recurrent cyanotic episodes after a provoking cry and the investigations that actually change management
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar. An 18 month old boy has had six episodes over three months in which he cries hard after a fall or a frustration, stops breathing in expiration, turns blue around the lips, goes limp and loses consciousness for about ten seconds. He then has a few jerks of all four limbs, wakes quickly and is back to normal within a minute.

Every episode has followed a bout of crying. His mother says he still drinks about a litre of cow milk a day and eats very little meat or vegetables. He is developmentally appropriate with a normal neurological examination and normal growth. His parents are frightened and want to know whether he is having fits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 116, blood pressure 94/58, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Normal tone, power and reflexes, no dysmorphic features, normal cardiovascular examination with no murmur, conjunctival pallor
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (110-140); mean cell volume 68 fL (75-87); ferritin 7 mcg/L (15-150)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start oral iron replacement and obtain a twelve lead electrocardiogram before discharge
options.rationale: Both actions are correct but this pairing omits the explanation and safety advice to the parents, which is the intervention that most reduces presentations and distress (Source: RCH CPG: Breath Holding Spells).

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram and start sodium valproate at an antiepileptic dose
options.rationale: Anoxic jerks following a provoked cyanotic episode are secondary to cerebral hypoperfusion rather than epileptic, so antiepileptic therapy treats the wrong mechanism (Source: RCH CPG: Breath Holding Spells).

options.text: Admit for overnight cardiac monitoring and arrange an echocardiogram in the morning
options.rationale: Structural cardiac assessment is warranted when episodes occur without a preceding cry or during exercise, and here every episode has followed hard crying with a normal cardiovascular examination (Source: RCH CPG: Breath Holding Spells).

options.text: Give parental explanation with safety advice, correct the iron deficiency, and record an electrocardiogram
options.rationale: The episodes are stereotyped breath holding spells, iron treatment reduces their frequency, and a single electrocardiogram excludes a long QT interval that can mimic them (Source: RCH CPG: Breath Holding Spells).

options.text: Reassure without investigation and review him in the general clinic in three months
options.rationale: Reassurance is central but the microcytic anaemia is a treatable driver of the spells and a prolonged QT interval is the one dangerous mimic that must be excluded (Source: RCH CPG: Breath Holding Spells).

explanation.summary: Breath holding spells affect up to 5 per cent of young children and are reflex events, not epilepsy, in which a provoking cry or fright is followed by apnoea in expiration, colour change, loss of tone and then loss of consciousness. Brief stiffening or a few clonic jerks follow in a substantial minority because of cerebral hypoperfusion, and these anoxic jerks are the reason the events are so often misdiagnosed as seizures. Iron deficiency is over represented in affected children and correcting it reduces spell frequency, which makes a full blood count and ferritin worthwhile even in a child who looks well. The one mimic that must not be missed is a channelopathy such as long QT syndrome, so a resting electrocardiogram is recommended, and any episode occurring without a provoking cry or during exertion should push the assessment towards a cardiac cause.
key_points: A provoking cry followed by apnoea, colour change and collapse is the defining sequence
Anoxic jerks after loss of consciousness do not make the event epileptic
Check full blood count and ferritin because iron deficiency increases spell frequency
Record an electrocardiogram to exclude a prolonged QT interval
Unprovoked or exertional events shift the differential towards a cardiac arrhythmia
explanation.pearls: Correcting iron deficiency with three to six months of oral iron reduces breath holding spell frequency substantially, so treat to a normal ferritin rather than stopping once the haemoglobin has recovered.

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic threshold and feeding advice in a lactating woman with a red painful breast
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A woman who gave birth three weeks ago presents with a hot painful area in the upper outer part of her right breast that she first noticed 18 hours ago after a long stretch between feeds. She has been shivery and aching since last night.

She has been feeding from that side but says it hurts so much she has started to skip it. There is a firm wedge shaped area of redness and tenderness in the upper outer quadrant with no fluctuance and no discrete lump. The nipple has a shallow fissure. There is no axillary lymphadenopathy and the overlying skin is not peeling or blistered.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.6
data_table.Examination: Wedge shaped erythema and induration in the right upper outer quadrant, no fluctuant collection, shallow nipple fissure, no axillary nodes
data_table.Investigations: Breast milk culture not routinely performed; ultrasound not yet arranged

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease feeding from the affected breast and express and discard the milk for 48 hours
options.rationale: Stopping drainage is what allows a simple inflammation to progress to abscess, and the milk remains safe for the infant even when the mother is receiving antibiotics (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Australian Breastfeeding Association).

options.text: Prescribe oral di or flucloxacillin, continue feeding from that breast and review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Symptoms beyond 12 to 24 hours with fever and a nipple fissure indicate bacterial infection rather than simple milk stasis, Staphylococcus aureus is the usual organism, and continued drainage is part of the treatment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Australian Breastfeeding Association).

options.text: Advise frequent feeding and cold packs alone and review her again in 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: Conservative management alone is appropriate for the first 12 to 24 hours of symptoms without fever, and it is now beyond that window with rigors and a portal of entry (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association).

options.text: Arrange a breast ultrasound today and withhold antibiotics until the result is available
options.rationale: Ultrasound is for suspected abscess, signalled by a fluctuant or discrete mass or by failure to improve after 48 hours of antibiotics, and deferring treatment for imaging now is unnecessary (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Prescribe oral cabergoline to suppress lactation and change the infant to formula feeding
options.rationale: Lactation suppression is used when a woman has decided to wean or after infant loss, and using it here removes both the drainage and the feeding relationship unnecessarily (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Lactational mastitis begins as inflammation from milk stasis, and only some cases progress to bacterial infection, which is why the first 12 to 24 hours of a red tender wedge without systemic upset are managed with effective drainage, cold packs and anti inflammatory analgesia. The features that shift the balance towards infection are persistence beyond that window, fever with rigors, and a cracked nipple providing a portal of entry for skin flora. Because Staphylococcus aureus predominates, an antistaphylococcal penicillin is first line and cefalexin or clindamycin is used in penicillin allergy. Continuing to feed or express from the affected side is not merely permitted but therapeutic, and the milk poses no risk to a healthy term infant.
key_points: Conservative management is appropriate only in the first 12 to 24 hours without systemic features
Fever with rigors and a nipple fissure indicate bacterial infection needing antibiotics
Di or flucloxacillin is first line, with cefalexin or clindamycin in penicillin allergy
Continue feeding or expressing from the affected breast throughout treatment
Failure to improve within 48 hours prompts ultrasound to look for an abscess
explanation.pearls: A woman whose mastitis has not improved after 48 hours of an appropriate antistaphylococcal penicillin needs a breast ultrasound the same day, since abscess is the reason for failure far more often than resistance.

subtopic_detail: Formulation and route of menopausal hormone therapy in a woman with migraine with aura and obesity
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 52 year old woman has not had a period for 16 months and has 12 or more hot flushes a day with drenching night sweats that wake her repeatedly. She has tried reducing caffeine and alcohol without benefit and says her work is suffering.

She has migraine with visual aura about twice a month, unchanged for years. Her body mass index is 34 kg/m2 and her blood pressure is 128/78. She has an intact uterus, has never had a venous thromboembolism, and has no personal or family history of breast cancer. Her cervical screening and mammogram are both up to date and normal. She asks specifically for something that will stop the flushes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 34 kg/m2, no breast masses, normal abdominal and pelvic examination
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test negative for human papillomavirus 8 months ago; mammogram normal 5 months ago

options.text: Oral conjugated equine oestrogen with continuous oral medroxyprogesterone acetate
options.rationale: An oral oestrogen passes through the liver and raises venous thromboembolism risk, which is the specific hazard being avoided in a woman with obesity and aura (Source: Australasian Menopause Society; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill containing 20 micrograms of ethinyloestradiol daily
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated by migraine with aura at any age because of the ischaemic stroke risk, and it delivers far more oestrogen than symptom control requires (Source: Australasian Menopause Society).

options.text: Oral venlafaxine titrated for vasomotor symptoms with review of the response in eight weeks
options.rationale: A serotonin noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor is the option when hormone therapy is contraindicated or declined, and it is less effective than oestrogen for flushes of this severity (Source: Australasian Menopause Society).

options.text: Transdermal oestradiol patch with continuous oral micronised progesterone at night
options.rationale: Transdermal oestradiol avoids first pass hepatic metabolism so it does not raise thromboembolic risk, migraine with aura does not contraindicate it, and an intact uterus requires progestogen for endometrial protection (Source: Australasian Menopause Society; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Transdermal oestradiol patch alone with an endometrial ultrasound every twelve months
options.rationale: Unopposed oestrogen in a woman with a uterus causes endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma, and surveillance scanning does not substitute for the progestogen that prevents it (Source: Australasian Menopause Society).

explanation.summary: Menopausal hormone therapy remains the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms, and the modern discussion is about route and formulation rather than whether to offer it at all. Transdermal oestradiol bypasses hepatic first pass metabolism, so unlike oral oestrogen it does not increase venous thromboembolism or stroke risk, which makes it the preferred route in women with obesity, migraine with aura, or other thrombotic risk factors. Any woman with an intact uterus needs a progestogen, and micronised progesterone is favoured over older synthetic progestogens because of a more favourable breast and cardiovascular profile. Migraine with aura contraindicates combined hormonal contraception because of the ethinyloestradiol dose, but it does not contraindicate physiological transdermal oestradiol replacement.
key_points: Transdermal oestradiol does not raise venous thromboembolism risk whereas oral oestrogen does
Migraine with aura contraindicates combined contraception but not transdermal replacement
An intact uterus always requires progestogen or a levonorgestrel intrauterine device
Micronised progesterone is the preferred progestogen for its breast and metabolic profile
Non hormonal options such as venlafaxine are second line when hormone therapy is unsuitable
explanation.pearls: A levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine device provides endometrial protection alongside transdermal oestradiol and is the practical choice when a woman also wants contraception in the perimenopause.

subtopic_detail: Emergency contraception method choice at the outer limit of the window with a high body mass index
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 26 year old woman who had unprotected intercourse 96 hours ago. Her cycles are regular at 28 days and today is day 13. Her body mass index is 36 kg/m2.

She says she does not want to be pregnant and would also like ongoing contraception she does not have to think about. She has no allergies, takes no regular medications and has had one previous uncomplicated vaginal birth. She has never had pelvic inflammatory disease. A urine pregnancy test today is negative and swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea have been taken.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 36 kg/m2, soft non tender abdomen, no cervical motion tenderness, uterus anteverted and normal size
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative; chlamydia and gonorrhoea nucleic acid testing pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate option to recommend?

options.text: Insert a copper intrauterine device today and treat presumptively if the swabs return positive
options.rationale: The copper device is effective up to five days after intercourse and is unaffected by body weight, and it simultaneously provides the long acting method she wants (Source: Family Planning Australia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give oral levonorgestrel 1.5 mg now and start a combined oral contraceptive tomorrow
options.rationale: Levonorgestrel is licensed only to 72 hours and its efficacy falls further with a body mass index above 26, so it is the weakest option in this specific situation (Source: Family Planning Australia).

options.text: Give oral ulipristal acetate 30 mg now and arrange an etonogestrel implant next week
options.rationale: Ulipristal does work to 120 hours but is less reliable at higher body weight than a copper device, and a progestogen started soon afterwards reduces its effect (Source: Family Planning Australia).

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine device today and repeat a pregnancy test in three weeks
options.rationale: The hormonal device is excellent ongoing contraception but does not reliably prevent implantation after intercourse has already occurred, which is what the copper device does (Source: Family Planning Australia).

options.text: Advise that the window has closed and arrange a pregnancy test in two weeks instead
options.rationale: The window for both ulipristal and the copper device extends to five days after intercourse, so emergency contraception is still available at 96 hours (Source: Family Planning Australia).

explanation.summary: Emergency contraception has three options in Australia and they differ in both time window and the effect of body weight. Levonorgestrel is licensed to 72 hours and loses efficacy above a body mass index of about 26, ulipristal acetate extends to 120 hours and performs better but is also weight sensitive, and the copper intrauterine device works to 120 hours with a failure rate under 1 per cent that is independent of weight. Where a woman also wants long acting contraception the copper device answers both questions in one visit, which is why it is the preferred recommendation when insertion is available. Pending sexually transmitted infection results do not delay insertion in an asymptomatic woman, since treatment can be given if the swabs return positive.
key_points: Copper intrauterine device is the most effective emergency method and works to 120 hours
Levonorgestrel is limited to 72 hours and loses efficacy with rising body mass index
Ulipristal extends to 120 hours but progestogen started soon afterwards reduces its effect
A levonorgestrel intrauterine device is not an emergency contraceptive
Asymptomatic pending swabs do not contraindicate same day insertion
explanation.pearls: If ulipristal acetate is used, wait five days before starting or restarting a progestogen containing method, because the progestogen competes at the receptor and undermines the ulipristal effect.

subtopic_detail: Perineal assessment after an apparently second degree tear and the consequence of understaging
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite after a spontaneous vaginal birth. A woman in her first pregnancy has just given birth to a 4100 g baby after a 40 minute second stage with a rotational forceps delivery. The midwife reports a tear she has graded as second degree and asks you to repair it in the room.

The perineal skin and the bulbospongiosus and transverse perineal muscles are torn. On systematic rectal examination with a finger in the anal canal and a thumb on the perineum, you can feel a gap in the fibres of the external sphincter over about a third of its circumference, and the internal sphincter is intact. There is no buttonhole into the rectal mucosa. Estimated blood loss is 350 mL.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88, blood pressure 116/70, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: Perineal body torn, partial defect of the external anal sphincter over less than half its thickness, internal anal sphincter and anorectal mucosa intact
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165); estimated blood loss 350 mL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repair the perineal muscles and skin in the birth suite under local anaesthetic infiltration
options.rationale: Repairing this as a second degree tear leaves the sphincter defect unopposed, and unrecognised sphincter injury is a leading cause of later faecal incontinence (Source: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

options.text: Pack the perineum, start intravenous antibiotics and plan a delayed repair in six weeks
options.rationale: Delayed repair is reserved for injuries recognised late or with gross contamination, and primary repair at the time of birth gives substantially better continence outcomes (Source: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

options.text: Transfer to theatre for repair by an experienced operator under regional or general anaesthesia
options.rationale: A partial external sphincter defect is a third degree tear, and outcomes depend on repair in theatre with adequate anaesthesia, lighting and assistance by an operator trained in sphincter repair (Source: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

options.text: Arrange an endoanal ultrasound scan in the ward before deciding on the mode of repair
options.rationale: Endoanal ultrasound has a role in later assessment of persisting symptoms, but the defect is already palpable and imaging only delays the primary repair (Source: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

options.text: Repair the tear in the birth suite and arrange colorectal review before she is discharged
options.rationale: Deferring the sphincter to a later specialist opinion accepts a suboptimal primary repair, which is the step that most determines long term continence (Source: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

explanation.summary: Obstetric anal sphincter injury is understaged when the perineum is inspected without a systematic rectal examination, and understaging is the single commonest reason a woman ends up with faecal incontinence after childbirth. The classification runs from 3a, less than half the external sphincter thickness, through 3b, more than half, to 3c, which involves the internal sphincter, and fourth degree, which breaches the anorectal mucosa. Risk factors are first vaginal birth, instrumental birth particularly with forceps, birthweight above 4 kg, prolonged second stage and occipitoposterior position. Repair belongs in theatre with regional or general anaesthesia so the sphincter ends can be identified and apposed, followed by broad spectrum antibiotics, laxatives to avoid straining on the repair, and physiotherapy with structured follow up.
key_points: Perform a rectal examination on every woman after vaginal birth before grading a tear
A partial external sphincter defect is 3a and a defect beyond half its thickness is 3b
Primary repair in theatre by a trained operator gives the best continence outcome
Instrumental birth, birthweight over 4 kg and first vaginal birth are the main risks
Postoperative care includes antibiotics, laxatives and pelvic floor physiotherapy
explanation.pearls: Prescribe a stool softener such as lactulose rather than a bulking agent after sphincter repair, since a bulky stool passing over a fresh repair is a recognised cause of early breakdown.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic confirmation before labelling ovarian insufficiency in a woman in her thirties
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in clinic. A 34 year old woman has had no periods for seven months after a lifetime of regular cycles. She has hot flushes at night and says intercourse has become uncomfortable. She and her partner had been planning a pregnancy this year.

She has never been pregnant, uses no hormonal contraception and stopped none recently. She has had no chemotherapy, radiotherapy or pelvic surgery. Her weight is stable, she exercises moderately and there is no excessive exercise or dietary restriction. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Blood taken three weeks ago showed follicle stimulating hormone 46 IU/L (2 to 10 in the follicular phase), oestradiol 48 pmol/L (110 to 400) and normal thyroid stimulating hormone and prolactin. She asks whether this means she is in menopause.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2, no galactorrhoea, no hirsutism or acanthosis, atrophic vaginal appearance, normal sized uterus
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone 46 IU/L (2-10 follicular); oestradiol 48 pmol/L (110-400); thyroid stimulating hormone and prolactin within normal limits; urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive pill and review her symptoms again in three months
options.rationale: Hormone replacement is needed eventually to protect bone and cardiovascular health, but starting it before the diagnostic samples are complete removes the ability to confirm the diagnosis (Source: RANZCOG: Premature Ovarian Insufficiency).

options.text: Arrange a pelvic ultrasound to count antral follicles and measure anti Mullerian hormone
options.rationale: Antral follicle count and anti Mullerian hormone estimate ovarian reserve for fertility planning but neither is a diagnostic criterion for this condition (Source: RANZCOG: Premature Ovarian Insufficiency).

options.text: Refer directly to a fertility service for donor oocyte counselling and treatment planning
options.rationale: Donor oocyte counselling becomes relevant once the diagnosis is confirmed, and spontaneous ovulation still occurs intermittently in this condition so the diagnosis must be secure first (Source: RANZCOG: Premature Ovarian Insufficiency).

options.text: Perform a progestogen withdrawal challenge and assess whether she has a withdrawal bleed
options.rationale: A withdrawal bleed distinguishes outflow tract obstruction from anovulation, a question already answered by a high follicle stimulating hormone with a low oestradiol (Source: RANZCOG: Premature Ovarian Insufficiency).

options.text: Repeat the follicle stimulating hormone and oestradiol at least four weeks apart to confirm
options.rationale: The diagnosis requires amenorrhoea for at least four months plus two raised follicle stimulating hormone results taken at least four weeks apart, because a single elevated value can reflect a transient rise (Source: RANZCOG: Premature Ovarian Insufficiency).

explanation.summary: Premature ovarian insufficiency is loss of ovarian function before the age of 40 and is diagnosed on amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea for at least four months together with two follicle stimulating hormone measurements in the menopausal range taken at least four weeks apart. The requirement for two samples exists because fluctuating gonadotrophins are common and a single high value can be transient, and the label carries lifelong consequences for bone density, cardiovascular risk and fertility. Once confirmed, the aetiological workup includes a karyotype, fragile X premutation testing and adrenal and thyroid autoantibodies, since Turner mosaicism, the FMR1 premutation and autoimmune polyglandular disease are all recognised causes. Hormone replacement is then continued until the average age of natural menopause rather than being viewed as optional symptom relief, and spontaneous conception remains possible in a small proportion so contraception must be discussed if pregnancy is not wanted.
key_points: Diagnosis needs two raised follicle stimulating hormone results at least four weeks apart
Amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea for at least four months is the other criterion
Confirmed cases need karyotype, fragile X premutation and autoantibody testing
Hormone replacement continues to about age 51 for bone and cardiovascular protection
Intermittent ovulation persists so contraception is still needed if pregnancy is unwanted
explanation.pearls: Around 5 to 10 per cent of women with confirmed premature ovarian insufficiency conceive spontaneously, so the diagnosis is never given as a statement that pregnancy is impossible.
